strengths: Addresses practical, well-motivated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation without fine-tuning or anomalous samples, valuable for real-world industrial deployment where defects are scarce and costly to curate.

Novel delta-denoising attribution mechanism that cleverly ties anomaly localization to diffusion model's own denoising dynamics by accumulating per-step latent discrepancies between normal and anomaly branches—more principled than prior attention-map-based approaches.

Comprehensive technical design combining normal-reference initialization, token-level prompt refinement (dual objectives for context alignment and semantic distillation), and spatial attention biasing. Each component is well-motivated and thoroughly ablated.

Thorough experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS, AUROC, AP) and comprehensive baseline comparison (DRAEM, DFMGAN, AnomalyDiffusion, AnoGen, AnomalyAny) with fair zero-shot protocol and no test-set leakage.

Strong empirical results: achieves highest generation quality metrics (IS=2.03, IC-LPIPS=0.36) and consistent improvements over ZSAG baseline AnomalyAny in downstream detection (mean AUROC 84.7 vs 77.6).

Clear presentation with effective qualitative visualizations (Figure 3) demonstrating sharper boundaries and better realism than prior methods, plus comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3, Figures 4–5) validating design choices.
Truly training-free and cross-category generalizable, enabling immediate practical deployment for rapid data bootstrapping in production environments.
weaknesses: Inconsistent category-level downstream performance: several categories degrade vs. AnomalyAny (cable AUCp 82.2→76.2; capsule AUCi 59.4→54.9; leather APp 45.0→47.1 with much lower image-level scores). Pixel-level AP gains are often marginal, and paper acknowledges method struggles with complex/fine-grained defects, limiting claims of general superiority.

Limited component-level novelty: normal-reference initialization, prompt refinement, and spatial attention biasing are incremental adaptations of existing diffusion-editing techniques. Primary contribution is the combination rather than fundamental methodological innovation.

Critical evaluation gaps: (1) Mask quality lacks direct quantitative evaluation (no F1/IoU vs. ground truth masks, only indirect downstream detection); (2) computational cost completely absent (two 100-step diffusion branches is expensive; no inference time comparison); (3) cross-dataset generalization missing from main paper—results on 'other datasets' relegated to appendix; (4) threshold choices (τmid=0.6, τfinal=0.35) lack sensitivity analysis and justification for split at tmid.

Prompt engineering dependence: success requires selecting appropriate anomaly descriptors per defect type; no systematic guidelines or sensitivity study provided. Real-world deployment requires domain expertise to determine suitable prompts for novel defect types.

External dependencies and failure modes: relies on SAM (Segment Anything Model) for foreground mask Mfg; impact of SAM failure on robustness not discussed. Hyperparameter choices (γ=0.3, T=100) lack justification or ablation.

Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic investigation of which defect categories/types fail systematically (e.g., do structural vs. surface defects behave differently?). Category-dependent variance (Table 2) suggests limited robustness but no diagnosis provided.

Acknowledged but unresolved limitations: controllability 'remains limited' per authors; evaluation protocols 'are limited and may require MLLM-based assessment'; generated anomalies are primarily 'structural or surface-level' while 'abstract or logical defects remain challenging.'

Reproducibility concerns: code not yet available; critical hyperparameters (T, γ, thresholds) lack ablation studies or principled selection; tied to Stable Diffusion v1.5 specifics, generalization to newer checkpoints unclear.

Notation and clarity: ⊙ operator used ambiguously for both element-wise and mask-guided operations; 'clean()' operation in Algorithm 1 undefined; relationship between masks (Mfg, Mmid, M) not sufficiently explicit.

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical problem: training-free zero-shot anomaly generation eliminates dependence on rare anomalous samples, solving a key limitation of few-shot methods.
Sensible technical design: the combination of delta-denoising attribution, mask-guided inpainting, and prompt refinement is well-motivated and clearly presented.
Comprehensive experimental framework: 15 MVTec categories with both generation metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS) and practical downstream detection evaluation.
Thorough ablations: visualizations and quantitative ablations (Table 3) demonstrate the contribution of each component.
Practical utility: a truly training-free approach that generates both anomalies and masks without fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: delta-denoising attribution is an incremental extension of DiffEdit [9]; mask-guided inpainting, attention biasing, and prompt refinement are existing techniques. The contribution is primarily an engineering combination rather than a novel mechanism.

Weak evaluation metrics: Inception Score is a problematic metric for image quality; IC-LPIPS is non-standard. Generation quality improvements are marginal (2.03 vs. 2.02 average IS). No human perceptual evaluation conducted.

Highly inconsistent downstream results: Table 2 shows large variance across categories. Cable improves dramatically (70.9 vs 44.1), while capsule (54.9 vs 59.4), metal_nut (73.8 vs 54.3), and grid (81.3 vs 85.7) degrade. Claims of 'consistent gains' are not supported; results appear unstable.

Unaddressed hyperparameter sensitivity: many hyperparameters (γ=0.3, τ_mid=0.6, τ_final=0.35, α_t, η, β) lack ablation or justification. Selection criteria unexplained. This undermines the 'training-free' claim.

Mask quality not rigorously evaluated: only visual comparisons provided; no quantitative pixel-level accuracy metrics against ground-truth anomalies. Unclear whether delta-denoising masks capture true anomaly locations or just salient regions.

Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Single-run results; unclear if stable across random seeds. Marginal differences (e.g., IS) cannot be interpreted without variance estimates.

Acknowledged but unresolved limitations: authors admit method generates only 'structural or surface-level characteristics' while 'more abstract or logical defects remain challenging.' This narrows real-world applicability.

Reproducibility gaps: description prompts for semantic distillation not explicitly specified for each category, suggesting category-specific tuning required. Threshold selection unjustified. SAM foreground mask dependency not analyzed.

Incomplete analysis: no failure case discussion, no sensitivity to multiple hyperparameters, limited generalization evidence beyond MVTec AD, no investigation of multi-region anomalies or complex defect patterns.

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses the real challenge of anomaly scarcity by proposing fully training-free zero-shot generation, eliminating dependence on expensive anomalous samples and enabling cross-category generalization

Coherent technical approach: elegantly combines delta-denoising localization, normal-reference initialization, mask-guided latent inpainting, token-level prompt refinement, and spatial attention biasing into a unified pipeline where components work synergistically

Thorough experimental validation: comprehensive evaluation on 15 MVTec AD categories with 73 anomaly types; fair ZSAG-to-ZSAG comparison; both generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS) and downstream detection effectiveness measured; detailed ablations demonstrating contribution of each component

Consistent downstream improvements: achieves higher detection performance than AnomalyAny baseline (AUCi: 84.7 vs 77.6, APi: 91.3 vs 87.1) with controlled generation from single guidance images per category

Clear presentation and reproducibility: well-written with effective visualizations (especially Figure 2), precise algorithm description (Algorithm 1), implementation details provided, and code release promised
Practical deployment advantages: training-free inference, no model adaptation required, no fine-tuning, strong cross-category generalization without category-specific overfitting
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: delta-denoising directly builds on DiffEdit, latent inpainting is standard, attention biasing follows Attend-and-Excite; contribution is primarily a skillful combination of existing techniques for a new application rather than fundamental innovation

Evaluation metrics not tailored to anomaly generation task: Inception Score and IC-LPIPS are general image quality metrics not designed to assess whether generated anomalies are realistic defects; downstream detection uses only simple U-Net; no perceptual evaluation or human assessment of defect realism and detectability

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and limitations: authors acknowledge that abstract/logical defects remain challenging but provide no examples, analysis, or guidance; significant performance variance across categories (e.g., cable AUCi 70.9 vs 44.1, screw shows minimal gains) is unexplained; no investigation of when delta-denoising breaks down

Critical prompt engineering dependency underexplored: method relies on carefully designed normal/anomaly prompts but sensitivity analysis is absent; no systematic study of prompt variations; unclear guidance for practitioners on designing prompts for new domains

SAM dependency introduces hidden assumption and external model coupling: foreground mask from Segment Anything Model may fail on domains where SAM performs poorly; this external dependency is not discussed or analyzed despite claimed training-free nature

Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: multiple hyperparameters (γ=0.3, τ_mid=0.6, τ_final=0.35, β for attention bias, η for loss balance, α for step size) lack ablation or sensitivity analysis; unclear if values are dataset or category-specific
Computational cost and efficiency not analyzed: no runtime comparison, memory requirements, or efficiency analysis provided despite running two synchronized diffusion branches for 100 steps

Limited cross-domain evaluation: most results on MVTec AD; while unseen categories within MVTec are tested, evaluation on fundamentally different domains (distinct industrial processes, materials, lighting conditions) would strengthen generalization claims
Defect diversity not thoroughly analyzed: no quantitative analysis of whether generated anomalies exhibit sufficient diversity or collapse to stereotypical patterns beyond IC-LPIPS metric

Token-level prompt refinement appears somewhat ad-hoc: semantic distillation and context alignment losses are hand-crafted with limited justification for design choices (e.g., why MSE for context alignment?); no comparison with alternative refinement strategies

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical scarcity of anomalous data with clear deployment motivation
Novel core concept (delta-denoising attribution) with intuitive design that leverages synchronized diffusion branches without supervision
Comprehensive experimental validation on two benchmarks (MVTec AD, VisA) with multiple evaluation perspectives and strong baselines
Each method component is well-justified with convincing ablations demonstrating necessity and contribution
Achieves competitive results with FSAG methods on some categories (89.7% AUCi with FLUX); outperforms some ZSAG baselines
Model-agnostic framework demonstrating transferability from Stable Diffusion v1.5 to FLUX.1-dev
Practical efficiency considerations with favorable runtime/memory compared to AnomalyAny
Refreshing transparency about evaluation protocol limitations and method constraints (acknowledged in Appendix D)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (latent inpainting, prompt refinement, attention biasing) are known; primary contribution is their combination for ZSAG
Acknowledged but consequential evaluation limitations: IC-LPIPS metrics fundamentally misaligned for ZSAG since they assume real anomaly anchors that zero-shot methods don't observe
Performance remains category-dependent with notable variance (cable: 70.9% AUCi; screw: 73.3% with only 4.7% APp), suggesting method brittleness
Threshold sensitivity (Table 6: range 78.8%–88.6% AUCi across T1 values) contradicts 'zero-shot' claim; universal defaults require empirical tuning
Hyperparameter choices lack justification (γ=0.3, β=4, η=4, λ=0.5); why L2 norm specifically in Eq. 8? No ablation on distance metrics
Two-threshold strategy (tmid vs. final) and accumulator reset at mid-denoising appear empirically motivated without principled justification
Marginal improvements over existing ZSAG baselines (e.g., Table 1: 2.05 vs. 2.02 IS; differences within noise given evaluation concerns)
Constrained scope: limited to structural/surface defects, prompt-based anomaly specification, SAM dependency despite claimed independence
Insufficient analysis: no feature-space comparison of synthesized vs. real anomaly distributions; limited failure mode discussion
Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable at review; many design decisions lack clear justification

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing zero-shot anomaly generation without real defective samples, relevant for industrial applications where defects are rare and costly to annotate
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on two datasets with extensive comparisons to both FSAG and ZSAG baselines, detailed ablation studies, and downstream detection validation

Achieves competitive performance with recent ZSAG methods and approaches FSAG methods using advanced backbones (FLUX), with good balance between generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS) and downstream utility
Thorough implementation documentation including Algorithm 1, detailed hyperparameter settings, runtime/memory analysis, SAM dependence ablation, and threshold sensitivity studies
Valuable critical discussion of evaluation protocol limitations in Appendix D, providing honest assessment of why current metrics may not appropriately measure ZSAG performance
Intuitive delta-denoising attribution concept that clearly captures semantic divergence between normal and anomaly branches through straightforward latent space comparison
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (branch comparison similar to DiffEdit, latent inpainting standard practice, token refinement via basic embedding optimization, spatial attention biasing combining known techniques) are largely adaptations rather than novel contributions; insufficient articulation of what is genuinely new versus incremental application

Weak theoretical justification for critical design choices: no principled explanation for L2 distance in latent space (vs. alternatives), linear accumulation in Eq. (9), binary thresholding in Eq. (10), or the two-stage early/late denoising split; these lack ablation or comparison studies

Self-contradictory evaluation: paper critiques IS and IC-LPIPS metrics as fundamentally flawed for ZSAG (Appendix D.1) yet reports these as primary results in Table 1; acknowledges downstream detection as 'coarse and confounded' (D.2) yet relies on it for main comparisons

Significant performance gap with FSAG methods on multiple categories despite ZSAG being compared fairly: cable (AnomalyDiffusion 99.5% vs. 70.9%), capsule (77.4% vs. 54.9%), screw (84.9% vs. 73.3%), undermining competitiveness claims

High variance across categories (capsule 54.9% AUCi vs. tile 99.9%) indicates poor generalization, but paper provides no systematic analysis of which category properties cause failure; vague explanation about 'complex or fine-grained patterns' without diagnostic evidence

Heavy reliance on external pre-trained models: SAM is critical (1.4% AUCi drop without it, contradicting 'self-contained' claims), Stable Diffusion/FLUX priors are foundational, generic prompt templates still require per-dataset customization despite 'dataset-agnostic' claims

Incomplete technical specification: Eq. (10) mentions 'light smoothing and normalization' without formal definition; Eq. (13) attention biasing interaction with softmax underspecified; no comparison of L2 aggregation to alternatives; two-stage design presented without justification ablation

Limited generalization scope: evaluated only on two industrial inspection datasets (MVTec AD, VisA); no evaluation on other domains, anomaly types, or real-world datasets outside manufacturing; transferability to other diffusion models unclear

No mask quality evaluation despite acknowledging its importance (Appendix D.3): only indirect assessment through downstream detection; missing direct metrics like mask precision, recall, boundary sharpness

Evaluation fairness issues: FSAG methods see real anomalies during fine-tuning, making comparison confounded; different backbone choices (SD v1.5 vs. FLUX) complicate direct comparisons; no statistical significance testing or error bars reported; no analysis of failure modes or category-specific weaknesses

strengths: Well-motivated zero-shot formulation addressing genuine industrial need for anomaly data without real defective samples
Sound technical approach combining delta-denoising attribution, normal-reference initialization, prompt refinement, and attention biasing in coherent framework

Comprehensive experimental validation across MVTec AD (15 categories) and VisA (12 categories) with multiple evaluation perspectives: generation quality, downstream detection, and qualitative assessment

Thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component, including module ablations, quantitative detection ablation, threshold sensitivity analysis, and semantic distillation visualization
Model-agnostic design successfully transferring from Stable Diffusion v1.5 to FLUX.1-dev without architecture-specific tuning
Honest and critical discussion in main text and appendix of limitations, evaluation protocol shortcomings, and future directions
weaknesses: Inconsistent and often marginal downstream detection improvements: category-dependent gains ranging from negligible to significant (e.g., cable 70.9% vs 44.1%, but capsule 54.9% vs 59.4% for AnomalyAny comparison); IS/IC-LPIPS metrics show only marginal advantages

Limited technical novelty: individual components (prompt contrasting from DiffEdit, attention manipulation, latent inpainting) are established techniques; contribution is primarily their specific combination rather than conceptual innovation

Insufficient justification for design choices: (1) no ablation on why L2 norm vs. other distance metrics; (2) T/2 midpoint strategy for accumulator reset lacks principled justification; (3) theoretical connection between latent-space discrepancies and semantic anomalies underdeveloped
Practical dependence on SAM contradicts 'training-free' framing: 1.4% AUCi performance drop without SAM (84.7%→83.3%), and SAM itself is trained on large-scale datasets, compromising zero-shot claim

Problematic evaluation choices: (1) IC-LPIPS metric inappropriate for ZSAG (anchors on real anomalies that model never observes); (2) one-shot single-image setting is artificial; (3) no cross-dataset transfer evaluation; (4) downstream detection entangles generator quality with detector architecture choices

Parameter tuning requirements: two thresholds (0.6, 0.35) require adjustment; different settings needed for FLUX vs. Stable Diffusion; prompt engineering requires dataset-specific anomaly terminology despite 'dataset-agnostic' claims
Limited controllability and scope: coarse semantic distillation control; acknowledged inability to generate abstract/logical defects; restricted to surface/structural defects
Runtime efficiency claims not compelling: 10.25 s/img with 10.36 GiB memory only marginally faster than AnoStyler (14.36 s) despite added complexity
